Before SAF can be utilized in flight, Federal Aviation Administration mandates require that fuel producers must undergo a rigorous approval process. This process, described in ASTM D4054, Standard Practice for Evaluation of New Aviation Turbine Fuels and Fuel Additives, was developed to ensure safe and reliable operation of aircraft on alternative aviation fuels (Holladay, et al. 2020). Passing the ASTM D4054 approval process requires that new fuel suppliers complete a four-tiered examination that involves physical property evaluation and live testing in engines. A summarized process is shown in Figure 7. Upon completion, a review and voting process is conducted to determine if the fuel is approved for commercial use. From start to finish, this approval process typically takes 3–5 years and cost in excess of $5 million (Holladay et al. 2020). 2 Standards are continuously updated; check the ASTM website for the latest version. 8 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Figure 7. Summary of new SAF pathway approval steps The current list of ASTM-approved SAF pathways is provided in Table 2, comprising eight distinct “annexes” to SAF and three coprocessing blends. As shown, current restrictions limit the blending of SAF to up to 50%, where the balance comprises conventional Jet A. Blending limits stem from both an abundance of conservatism surrounding the widespread use of relatively untested fuel(s) but also to ensure inclusion of key aromatic molecules which are notably absent across many of the prominent SAF pathways. Relaxing the blend limit to eventually utilize up to 100% SAF for some pathways will be dependent on either (1) modifications to existing and new aircraft engines that remove the need for aromatic-based O-ring swelling, or (2) the production of “compositionally complete” SAF fuels—such as via catalytic thermohydrolysis—that individually produce all required chemical families to meet performance benchmarks (c.f., Figure 3). Broadly, the approved pathways for SAF encompass five distinct chemical reaction pathways: (1) Fischer-Tropsch (FT), (2) hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA), (3) synthetic isoparaffins (SIP), (4) alcohol-to-jet (ATJ from both ethanol and isobutanol), and (5) catalytic hydrothermolysis (CH). While not yet approved, other emerging pathways are also under consideration, including waste and biomass pyrolysis and methanol-to-jet (MTJ) (ICAO 2025a).
